## Two credit questions: price changes and payment failures

<div class="comparison"><div><h3>Spread exposure</h3><p>How much does price change when the market demands different credit compensation? A bond can lose value without defaulting.</p></div><div><h3>Default exposure</h3><p>How likely is default, what will recovery be, and how do defaults cluster across a portfolio?</p></div></div>

$$
y_{corp}\approx y_{Treasury}+s
$$

## Corporate bond risk has several sources

![](lec3-11-assets/lec10-fig-credit-risk-map.svg){.figure}

## Absolute and relative spread changes answer different questions

$$
s_i=y_i-y_{Treasury}
$$

<div class="comparison"><div><h3>Absolute shock</h3><p>Δs: how many basis points does the spread move?</p></div><div><h3>Relative shock</h3><p>Δs / s: how large is the move compared with the starting spread?</p></div></div>

A move from 100 to 150 bp is +50 bp and +50%.

## Example 1 — the same 25 bp move has different meaning

| Bond | Starting spread | Absolute widening | Relative widening |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| A | 50 bp | 25 bp | 25 / 50 = 50% |
| B | 500 bp | 25 bp | 25 / 500 = 5% |

A’s required credit compensation increases by half. B’s proportional shock is much smaller.

## Compare absolute and proportional shocks visually

![](lec3-11-assets/lec10-fig-absolute-relative-spreads.svg){.figure}

Wider-spread bonds tend to experience larger basis-point moves, supporting proportional spread-risk measures.

## Spread duration holds Treasury rates constant

Hold the Treasury spot curve $\{r_t\}$ and promised payments $CF_t$ fixed. Shift the same spread $s$ at every maturity:
$$
P(s)=\sum_t\frac{CF_t}{(1+r_t+s)^t},\qquad
D_s=-\frac1{P_0}\frac{\partial P}{\partial s}
\approx\frac{P_--P_+}{2P_0\Delta s}.
$$

- $P_-=P(s-\Delta s)$, $P_+=P(s+\Delta s)$, and $P_0=P(s)$. Use a small positive bump $\Delta s$ in decimal units.
- For a spread move $\Delta s$, the first-order return is $\Delta P/P\approx-D_s\Delta s$ **with Treasury rates held fixed**.

## Example 2 — convert a spread shock into a price change

| Position | Spread widening | Price change | Result |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Price 98, $D_s=6.5$ | 40 bp | $-6.5(0.0040)=-2.60\%$ | $98(1-0.026)=95.45$ |
| Value $4 million, $D_s=4.5$ | 35 bp | $-4.5(0.0035)=-1.575\%$ | Loss of $63,000 |

The dollar loss is $4{,}000{,}000(0.01575)=63{,}000$ dollars. Both estimates hold Treasury rates fixed.

## DTS combines spread level and sensitivity

$$
\frac{\Delta P_{spread}}P\approx -D_s\Delta s
=-(D_s s)\frac{\Delta s}{s}
=-DTS\frac{\Delta s}{s}.
$$

A bond with $D_s=4$ and $s=90$ bp has $DTS=4(0.0090)=0.036$.

<div class="comparison"><div><h3>Spread duration</h3><p>Compare bonds using the same basis-point widening.</p></div><div><h3>DTS</h3><p>Compare bonds using the same percentage widening from each bond’s starting spread.</p></div></div>

## Example 3 — shorter duration can still mean more spread risk

Apply the same **20% relative widening** to both bonds.

| Bond | Spread duration | Starting spread | DTS | Absolute widening | Estimated return |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| A | 7.0 | 100 bp | .0700 | 20 bp | $-0.0700(0.20)=-1.40\%$ |
| B | 3.5 | 400 bp | .1400 | 80 bp | $-0.1400(0.20)=-2.80\%$ |

B’s starting spread more than offsets its shorter spread duration.

## Keep DTS quote units explicit

Worked examples:

| Spread duration | Spread | DTS in bp units | DTS in decimals |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 4.5 | 180 bp | 810 | .081 |
| 5.0 | 60 bp | 300 | .030 |
| 5.0 | 300 bp | 1,500 | .150 |

Divide bp-unit DTS by 10,000 before multiplying by a relative spread shock.

## Example 4 — locate portfolio spread risk

$$
\text{DTS contribution}_i=w_iD_{spread,i}s_i
$$

| Sector | Weight | Spread duration | Spread | DTS | Contribution to DTS |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| A-rated industrials | 50% | 6.0 | 1.20% | 7.20% | 3.60% |
| BBB financials | 30% | 5.0 | 2.00% | 10.00% | 3.00% |
| High yield | 20% | 3.0 | 5.00% | 15.00% | 3.00% |

Portfolio DTS = 3.60% + 3.00% + 3.00% = **9.60%**.

## Market weights can hide credit-risk concentration

![](lec3-11-assets/lec10-fig-portfolio-dts.svg){.figure}

The 20% high-yield allocation contributes as much DTS as the 30% BBB allocation. Both chart series are in percentage points, but measure different objects.

## Corporate bonds combine rates, spreads and equity-like risk

<div class="comparison"><div><h3>Higher quality</h3><p>Promised payments are more likely; Treasury-rate moves often dominate day-to-day price changes.</p></div><div><h3>Lower quality</h3><p>Default, recovery, refinancing and business outlook become more important; returns can behave more like equity.</p></div></div>

## A promised-cash-flow duration can overstate Treasury exposure

If credit spreads tighten when Treasury yields rise, the spread gain offsets some rate loss. Default/recovery expectations can also dominate the price.

$$
5\times0.25=1.25
$$

A 75% haircut brings an analytical duration of 5 down to 1.25. A historical empirical estimate is more explicit, but remains sample dependent.

## Analytical versus empirical duration

<div class="comparison"><div><h3>Analytical</h3><p>Compute sensitivity from promised cash flows, price, yield and maturity.</p></div><div><h3>Empirical</h3><p>Estimate actual bond-price behavior against Treasury yield changes.</p></div></div>

$$
\frac{\Delta P_t}{P_t}=\alpha-D_{\mathrm{emp}}\Delta y_t+\epsilon_t
$$

## The regression can be much flatter for high yield

![](lec3-11-assets/lec10-fig-empirical-duration-regression.svg){.figure}

## Two-factor price approximation

$$
\frac{\Delta P}{P}\approx -D\Delta y-Ds\frac{\Delta s}{s},
\qquad \mathrm{DTS}=Ds.
$$

- **Treasury effect:** $-D\Delta y$, where $\Delta y$ is the change in Treasury yield.
- **Spread effect:** $-\mathrm{DTS}\,\Delta s/s$, where $s$ is the starting spread and $\Delta s/s$ is its relative change.

**Why the same $D$?** With fixed cash flows discounted at one yield $y+s$, a 1 bp change in either component raises the total yield by 1 bp, holding the other fixed. Here $D$ is modified duration with respect to that total yield. This equality is model-specific.

## Divide by the Treasury yield change

For a nonzero Treasury yield move, divide by $\Delta y$ and factor out $-D$:

$$
\frac{1}{P}\frac{\Delta P}{\Delta y}
\approx -D-Ds\frac{\Delta s/s}{\Delta y}
= -D\left[1+s\frac{\Delta s/s}{\Delta y}\right].
$$

Estimate the typical relative spread response by regressing $\Delta s/s$ on $\Delta y$:

$$
\beta=\frac{\operatorname{cov}(\Delta y,\Delta s/s)}{\operatorname{var}(\Delta y)}
=\frac{\rho_{y,s}\sigma_y\sigma_s}{\sigma_y^2}
=\rho_{y,s}\frac{\sigma_s}{\sigma_y}.
$$

Use the **regression slope**, not an average of individual ratios. $\sigma_s$ measures relative spread changes; $\sigma_y$ measures Treasury yield changes.

## Spread co-movement changes empirical duration

Substitute the estimated spread response. Empirical duration is the negative of the estimated price response to Treasury yields:

$$
\frac{1}{P}\frac{\Delta P}{\Delta y}
\approx -D\left[1+s\rho_{y,s}\frac{\sigma_s}{\sigma_y}\right]
\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad
D_{\mathrm{emp}}\approx D\left[1+s\rho_{y,s}\frac{\sigma_s}{\sigma_y}\right].
$$

- **Negative correlation:** spreads tend to tighten as Treasury yields rise. The spread gain offsets some of the rate loss, and the multiplier is below 1.
- **Positive correlation:** spreads tend to widen as Treasury yields rise. The two losses reinforce each other, and the multiplier is above 1.

## Example 5 — calculate the multiplier

$D=6.0$, $s=3.00\%=0.0300$, $\rho_{y,s}=-0.50$, $\sigma_s=2.00\%=0.0200$ (relative spread changes), $\sigma_y=0.20\%=0.0020$ (Treasury yield changes).

1. **Estimate the spread response:** $\beta=\rho_{y,s}(\sigma_s/\sigma_y)=(-0.50)(0.0200/0.0020)=-5$.
2. **Adjust the duration:** $M=1+s\beta=1+0.0300(-5)=0.85$; $D_{\mathrm{emp}}=DM=6.0(0.85)=5.10$.

| For a 50 bp Treasury rise | Predicted bond price change |
|---|---:|
| Spread held fixed | $\Delta P/P\approx-6.0(0.0050)=-3.00\%$ |
| With estimated spread response | $\Delta P/P\approx-5.10(0.0050)=-2.55\%$ |

The estimated tightening offsets 0.45 percentage points of the rate loss.

## Example 6 — see the offset directly

Analytical duration $D=6$. Treasury yields rise **50 bp** while spreads tighten **30 bp**.

| Component | Estimated price change |
|---|---:|
| Treasury move | $-6(0.0050)=-3.0\%$ |
| Spread move | $-6(-0.0030)=+1.8\%$ |
| Combined | $-3.0\%+1.8\%=-1.2\%$ |

The implied sensitivity in **this scenario** is $1.2\%/0.50\%=2.4$. It is not a regression estimate, and the bond’s maturity has not changed.

## Duration multipliers summarize the empirical adjustment

$$
D_{\mathrm{emp}}\approx MD_{analytical},\qquad M=a+bs
$$

Rating and spread help explain multipliers. Wider-spread and lower-rated bonds often have smaller M; strong offsets can produce zero or negative empirical sensitivity.

With $M=0.65$ and $D=6$, adjusted duration is $0.65(6)=3.9$.

## Estimate multipliers in three stages

1. **Time series:** Estimate $D_{\mathrm{emp},i}$ for each bond from its price response to Treasury yield changes.
2. **Bond ratio:** Divide empirical by analytical duration, $M_i=D_{\mathrm{emp},i}/D_{\mathrm{analytical},i}$.
3. **Cross section:** Within a rating group, regress the bond-level multipliers on spreads, $M_i=a+bs_i+u_i$.

## Example 7 — size adjusted Treasury exposure

Hold $10 million of a B-rated bond, analytical duration 5, multiplier .25; Treasury shock +75 bp.

$$
D_{adjusted}=0.25(5)=1.25
$$

| Method | Return estimate | Dollar loss |
|---|---:|---:|
| Analytical | −5(.0075) = −3.75% | $375,000 |
| Adjusted | −1.25(.0075) = −.9375% | $93,750 |

Using unadjusted duration to size the hedge could overhedge Treasury risk. Issuer-specific spread risk remains.

## Example 8 — the apparent portfolio position can reverse

Target duration 5.5. Hold 85% at duration 5.8 and 15% high yield at analytical duration 5.0. With a high-yield multiplier of $0.25$, the adjusted high-yield duration is $5.0\times0.25=1.25$.

$$
D_{analytical,p}=0.85(5.8)+0.15(5.0)=5.68
$$

$$
D_{adjusted,p}=0.85(5.8)+0.15(1.25)=5.1175\approx5.12
$$

The adjusted portfolio is below target rather than above it. Adjusted duration is estimated and can change.

## The rating pattern is illustrative, not universal

![](lec3-11-assets/lec10-fig-duration-multipliers.svg){.figure}

These multipliers are separate illustrative assumptions, not the .25 B-rated input used in Examples 7–8. Estimates depend on rating, sector, maturity and market regime.

## Why credit risk is harder to model

<div class="comparison"><div><h3>Sparse observations</h3><p>Defaults are rare, particularly in investment grade; there is less event data than daily rate data.</p></div><div><h3>Heterogeneous issuers</h3><p>Industry, leverage, scale, assets, management, accounting, jurisdiction and funding structures differ.</p></div></div>

## Default causes and recovery vary across cycles

<div class="comparison"><div><h3>Many routes to default</h3><p>Poor management, leverage, fraud, commodities, litigation, recession, rates or a liquidity shock.</p></div><div><h3>Uncertain recovery</h3><p>Law, collateral, seniority, restructuring negotiations and market conditions determine loss.</p></div></div>

A model that works in one credit cycle may fail in another.

## Credit models serve three connected tasks

<div class="flow"><span><b>Default probabilities</b>One-year, five-year or full term structure</span><i>→</i><span><b>Pricing</b>Recovery, risk-free curve and risk compensation</span><i>→</i><span><b>Portfolio risk</b>Dependence and clustered defaults</span></div>

A portfolio of 100 bonds is not merely 100 independent default probabilities.

## Example 9 — expected loss is only a starting point

$$
EL=PD\times LGD=2\%\times60\%=1.2\%
$$

With a 4% risk-free yield, a naive expected-loss spread is 120 bp. That does not establish the fair market spread.

$$
\text{Spread}\approx\text{default compensation}+\text{risk/liquidity premiums}+\text{other effects}
$$

## Ratings and models provide different information

| Feature | Credit ratings | Credit risk models |
|---|---|---|
| Scale | Discrete grades | Continuous probabilities |
| Update frequency | Infrequent | Can update daily or intraday |
| Horizon | Often broad short-term or long-term view | Can produce maturity-specific default probabilities |
| Inputs | Fundamental review and agency judgment | Market data, accounting data, macro variables, model assumptions |
| Strength | Stable, widely understood benchmark | Timely, granular, useful for pricing and risk |
| Weakness | Slow-moving and coarse | Model risk and calibration risk |

## Structural default starts with the firm’s balance sheet

<div class="flow"><span><b>Firm assets</b>Market value and volatility</span><i>→</i><span><b>Debt obligations</b>Amount and maturity</span><i>→</i><span><b>Default threshold</b>Assets insufficient to meet the obligation</span></div>

Default is endogenous: it arises from the modeled capital structure.

## The basic BSM setup has one debt maturity

Assets A(t); one zero-coupon debt issue with face K due at T. Equity holders repay or default at maturity.

$$
\text{Default at }T\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad A(T)<K
$$

$$
PD=\Pr[A(T)<K]
$$

A lognormal asset process places some probability mass below the debt threshold.

## Asset paths show why the terminal threshold matters

![](lec3-11-assets/lec10-fig-bsm-asset-paths.svg){.figure}

Illustrative simulation: A₀ = 110, K = 100, μ = 4%, σ = 28%, T = 1. Basic BSM allows default only at maturity.

## Equity is a call option on firm assets

$$
E(T)=\max[A(T)-K,0]
$$

$$
B(T)=A(T)-\max[A(T)-K,0]
$$

Shareholders keep residual value when assets exceed debt; limited liability permits them to walk away below the threshold.

## Risky debt is a risk-free claim minus a default put

$$
B(T)=K-\max[K-A(T),0]=\min[A(T),K]
$$

The default put removes value from the promised debt payoff in low-asset-value states.

## Example 10 — allocate the terminal firm value

| Asset value at maturity | Equity payoff | Debt payoff |
|---:|---:|---:|
| 140 | 40 | 100 |
| 100 | 0 | 100 |
| 70 | 0 | 70 |

K = 100. At A(T) = 70, shareholders receive zero and bondholders recover 70 of the promised 100.

## The payoff diagram unifies debt and equity

![](lec3-11-assets/lec10-fig-bsm-payoffs.svg){.figure}

## Leverage and volatility connect to credit spreads

<div class="comparison"><div><h3>More leverage</h3><p>Higher K relative to A₀ moves the firm closer to the default threshold.</p></div><div><h3>More asset uncertainty</h3><p>Wider asset-value outcomes can increase downside risk and the default put’s value.</p></div></div>

For the solvent-firm setting emphasized in the notes, higher asset volatility generally raises default risk; the probability relationship is not universal across all leverage/drift settings.

## Structural models explain incentives but need difficult inputs

<div class="comparison"><div><h3>Economic strengths</h3><p>Connect credit to leverage, assets and volatility; analyze borrowing, equity issuance and risk shifting.</p></div><div><h3>Practical weaknesses</h3><p>Assets and volatility are inferred; complex debt, uncertain barriers and unstable calibration complicate implementation.</p></div></div>

Maturity-only default can understate short-horizon risk. An uncertain first-passage barrier is one way to allow default before maturity.

## Reduced-form models specify default arrival directly

<div class="flow"><span><b>Default time</b>An intensity or hazard process</span><i>→</i><span><b>Recovery</b>A recovery amount and timing rule</span><i>→</i><span><b>Discounting</b>A risk-free rate process</span></div>

Default is exogenous to a detailed asset/debt model. Market-price calibration makes this framework useful for trading and pricing.

## Poisson arrival logic over a very short interval

$$
\Pr(N_{t+dt}-N_t=1)\approx\lambda dt
$$

$$
\Pr(N_{t+dt}-N_t=0)\approx1-\lambda dt
$$

λ is conditional default intensity given survival. The approximation λdt applies only over a short interval. τ denotes the first default time.

## Intensity determines survival and cumulative default

$T$ is the time horizon (e.g., bond maturity); $\tau$ is the random time of default.

$$
\Pr(\tau>T)=e^{-\lambda T}
$$

$$
\Pr(\tau\le T)=1-e^{-\lambda T}
$$

With constant λ, the first Poisson arrival is default. A generic event-count process can have many arrivals; a single issuer defaults at the first one.

## Poisson event counts change shape with intensity

![](lec3-11-assets/lec10-fig-poisson-distributions.svg){.figure}

Over one time unit, N₁ ∼ Poisson(λ): mean = variance = λ. Larger intensity shifts mass right and makes the distribution less skewed.

## Higher intensity means faster average count growth

![](lec3-11-assets/lec10-fig-poisson-process-simulations.svg){.figure}

Paths are random and need not be ordered at every instant. These are event counts, not repeated defaults of one issuer.

## Example 11 — five-year survival with a 2% intensity

$$
S(5)=e^{-0.02(5)}=e^{-0.10}=90.48\%
$$

$$
PD(5)=1-90.48\%=9.52\%
$$

This is not exactly 2% × 5 = 10%. At one year: survival e⁻⁰·⁰² = 98.02%; intensity is not exactly one-year PD.

## Compare survival curves across hazard rates

![](lec3-11-assets/lec10-fig-poisson-survival.svg){.figure}

## Jarrow–Turnbull: default, recovery and migration

This simple version pays recovery at maturity, simplifying recovery-timing dependence. Extensions allow migration among rating states such as A, BBB, BB and default.

Transition matrices add credit-migration risk; recovery at maturity is unrealistic for many actual defaults.

## Duffie–Singleton: fractional recovery of market value

<div class="flow"><span><b>Before default</b>The risky bond has market value Vτ₋</span><i>→</i><span><b>At default</b>Recover a fraction of that value</span><i>→</i><span><b>Pricing</b>Combine intensity, recovery and rates</span></div>

Recovery occurs at default time and is tied to pre-default market value, rather than being allowed to exceed that value through an unrelated fixed amount.

## Compare the model families

| Issue | Structural models | Reduced-form models |
|---|---|---|
| Default driver | Firm value relative to debt | Exogenous default intensity |
| Main strength | Economic explanation | Market calibration and pricing |
| Main weakness | Hard inputs and calibration | Less economic explanation |
| Common use | Credit analysis, capital structure insight | Trading, pricing, credit derivatives |

Reduced-form calibration can infer credit/default curves from risky zeros, bonds and credit derivatives, but explains less about the economic cause of default.

## Recovery conventions change valuation

Recovery may be specified as a fraction of face value, pre-default market value, or a default-free equivalent claim.

Seniority, collateral, industry and the cycle affect realized recovery. A default probability alone does not determine price.

## Portfolio credit risk requires a dependence model

Common macro, industry, funding and liquidity shocks make defaults cluster. A linear correlation coefficient may not describe asymmetric tail outcomes.

A supplier’s reliance on an automaker illustrates asymmetric economic exposure; correlation itself is symmetric and does not establish causal direction.

## Copulas join marginal distributions into joint behavior

<div class="flow"><span><b>Marginals</b>Each issuer’s default distribution</span><i>→</i><span><b>Dependence</b>Specify how defaults occur together</span><i>→</i><span><b>Portfolio losses</b>Evaluate joint and tail outcomes</span></div>

A copula separates individual risk from dependence assumptions. Tail dependence is difficult to estimate and can be understated.

## Example 12 — expected loss stays the same

100 equal-sized bonds; each has one-year PD 2%; LGD 60%.

$$
E[\text{defaults}]=100(0.02)=2
$$

$$
EL=2(0.60)(0.01)=1.2\%
$$

Ten defaults are unlikely under independence but can become plausible under a shared recession factor.

## The same marginal PD can conceal very different tails

![](lec3-11-assets/lec10-default-dependence.svg){.figure}

Two-state example: 90% calm state with PD 0%; 10% stress state with conditional PD 20%. Unconditional PD remains 2%; expected defaults remain 2.

Defaults are independent conditional on the state. The chance of losing at least 6% is **0.0034%** with independent defaults versus **9.98%** with the common stress state; expected loss is 1.2% in both.

## Read empirical model comparisons with care

<div class="comparison"><div><h3>Ratings and structural models</h3><p>Ratings contain information but are coarse. Structural leverage, value and volatility help explain distress.</p></div><div><h3>Reduced-form models</h3><p>Timely market/accounting inputs can improve prediction and pricing, conditional on specification, calibration and data.</p></div></div>

Compare out-of-sample results before choosing a model.

## Relative value asks what spread compensates for

$$
\text{Spread-to-PD ratio}=\frac{\text{credit spread}}{\text{maturity-matched default probability}}
$$

Higher values mean more spread per unit of modeled default probability, all else equal. This is a comparison screen, not a complete pricing model.

## Example 13 — the wider spread is not automatically better

| Bond | Credit spread | Five-year default probability | Spread / default probability |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Bond A | 120 bps | 2.0% | 60 |
| Bond B | 180 bps | 6.0% | 30 |

The ratio is quoted in **bp of spread per percentage point of PD**: 120 / 2 = 60 and 180 / 6 = 30. With both inputs in decimals, the ratios are .60 and .30; rankings are unchanged.

## Compare compensation consistently across bonds

![](lec3-11-assets/lec10-fig-spread-pd-ratio.svg){.figure}

The chart also shows C: 90 bp / 1.5% and D: 250 bp / 10%. Liquidity, recovery, covenants, seniority, tax treatment and model error still matter.

## Incomplete information can hide proximity to default

<div class="comparison"><div><h3>Hidden obligations</h3><p>Off-balance-sheet items, derivatives, pensions and leases.</p></div><div><h3>Hidden condition</h3><p>Asset-quality problems, fraud, aggressive accounting and the true default barrier.</p></div></div>

Investors observe noisy signals rather than the firm’s complete economic condition.

## Bridge structural intuition and surprise default

<div class="flow"><span><b>Economic structure</b>Assets approach a default barrier</span><i>→</i><span><b>Incomplete information</b>Investors do not know the exact barrier</span><i>→</i><span><b>Observed default</b>Failure can arrive as a surprise</span></div>

A first-passage model with an uncertain barrier combines structural intuition with reduced-form features.

## In practice, calibrate a hazard curve to prices

<div class="flow"><span><b>Observe</b>Bond or CDS prices/spreads</span><i>→</i><span><b>Assume</b>Recovery amount and process</span><i>→</i><span><b>Calibrate</b>Term structure λ(t)</span><i>→</i><span><b>Value</b>Less-liquid bonds, loans or derivatives</span></div>

## A zero-recovery risky discount factor

$$
P_{risky}(0,T)\approx\exp\left[-\int_0^T(r(t)+\lambda(t))dt\right]
$$

In the simple deterministic-rate/intensity setting, hazard acts as an additional discount rate. Stochastic models require the corresponding risk-neutral expectation. Recovery changes the valuation equation.

## A spread–hazard shortcut needs assumptions

$$
s\approx\lambda\times LGD
$$

$$
0.02(1-0.40)=0.012=120\text{ bp}
$$

Pricing intensities are calibrated risk-neutral quantities; raw market spreads can also contain liquidity and other effects.

## Factor-driven hazard rates use issuer and macro information

$$
\lambda(t\mid X_t)=g(\beta_0+\beta^\top X_t)
$$

X can contain leverage, equity volatility, spreads, rating, unemployment and sector conditions. The link function g must produce a nonnegative intensity.

## A positive link prevents impossible intensities

$$
\lambda=\beta_0+\beta^\top X_t\quad\text{can be negative}
$$

$$
\lambda=\exp(\beta_0+\beta^\top X_t)>0
$$

Softplus is another positive link. A convenient statistical formula alone does not guarantee consistent asset prices.

## Arbitrage-free pricing requires a consistent framework

<div class="flow"><span><b>Measure</b>Specify risk-neutral dynamics</span><i>→</i><span><b>Intensity</b>Keep λ(t) nonnegative</span><i>→</i><span><b>Cash flows</b>Treat default and recovery consistently</span><i>→</i><span><b>Calibration</b>Fit traded prices</span></div>

A naive linear hazard model can violate these requirements.

## Physical and risk-neutral probabilities serve different uses

<div class="comparison"><div><h3>Physical PD</h3><p>Real-world default forecasting, expected loss, limits, underwriting, stress tests and capital planning.</p></div><div><h3>Risk-neutral PD</h3><p>Market-consistent valuation of bonds and credit derivatives.</p></div></div>

Market pricing includes systematic credit risk, liquidity and recovery uncertainty, especially losses in adverse states.

## Physical PD estimation uses several kinds of evidence

| Information | Examples |
|---|---|
| Default history | Defaults and rating transitions |
| Balance sheet | Leverage, profitability, liquidity, coverage |
| Market | Equity returns/volatility, bond and CDS spreads |
| Macro and sector | Growth, unemployment, rates, inflation, commodities, refinancing |

Common tools: logistic regression, survival models, transition matrices and panel models.

## Example 14 — distinguish expected loss from market spread

$$
PD_{physical}=1\%,\qquad R=40\%
$$

$$
EL=1\%(1-40\%)=0.60\%=60\text{ bp}
$$

The observed spread may be 150 bp. Risk premiums, liquidity, recovery uncertainty, taxes and supply/demand can account for the gap; a price-calibrated model may imply a higher risk-neutral PD.

## Turn measurements into a credit decision

<div class="flow"><span><b>Position</b>Instrument, seniority and spread measure</span><i>→</i><span><b>Exposure</b>Spread duration, DTS and rate scenarios</span><i>→</i><span><b>Credit</b>PD, recovery and dependence</span><i>→</i><span><b>Decision</b>Limit, hedge or relative value</span></div>

Model outputs organize judgment. Check liquidity, optionality, covenants, technical pressure and model risk before treating a wide spread as attractive.
